Nothing in the API says "reads only". The rules that make it unsuitable for writes are the same rules that make it so pleasant for reads, which is why they're easy to miss.
A resource describes data, not an action
The resource guide describes a resource as a way to bring async data into signal-based code, and its loader as a function that "retrieves some state". An

is a declaration: this component needs the data at this URL, for the current values of these signals. Angular decides when to send the request. A save is the opposite: an action the user decides to take, at one specific moment, exactly once.
It sends without waiting for anyone
: nothing goes out until something subscribes. The
guide spells out the difference: it "initiates the request eagerly". A resource with
when it's created, with whatever body the signals hold at that moment. In the opening story, that was an empty draft, sent before the profile had even loaded.
Every signal you read is a trigger
The request function is tracked like a
. The guide says that whenever one of the signals it depends on changes, the resource "will emit a new http request". That includes the body. Read
there, and every keystroke is a save. Read a locale signal for a header, and switching the language saves again. You can bolt on a "submitted" signal and return
until the click, but then you're rebuilding a click handler out of reactive parts, and you still inherit the next rule.
Cancelling is right for reads and risky for writes

"If a request is already pending, the resource cancels the outstanding request before issuing a new one." For a read, that's ideal: the older response is stale, so dropping it prevents a slow answer from overwriting a fresh one. For a write, cancelling only means the browser stops waiting. The request may already have reached the server and been saved, and now you have lost its response, its error and the knowledge of which version won. It's
behavior built in, and you can't swap it for queueing or ignoring the second click.

content.text: "canceled" in the Network panel means the browser stopped waiting for the response. It says nothing about the server, which may have received the full request and committed it. Never rely on cancellation to undo a write.
